design_detail: Letter to the editor (Drugs, 4 pages) commenting on the systematic review update by Evoy et al. (2021). Three authors: two psychiatrists in addiction medicine at the University of Duisburg-Essen (Bonnet, Scherbaum; authors of a 2017 systematic review on the same question) and an anaesthesiologist in pain medicine (McAnally). It argues from the review's own limitations, from a PubMed search for mediation analyses, from the authors' own studies (a 400-patient German elderly hospital sample; ratings of harms and benefits by German addiction physicians) and from cited reviews of gabapentinoids in withdrawal treatment. No systematic search, no data collected for the letter, no appraisal of individual studies.
can_establish: What the published critique says the review got wrong or left out (causal language from observational data, generalization from opioid-dependent samples, surrogate outcomes, the near absence of treatment seeking for gabapentinoid addiction, omitted benefits), and the authors' own figures as they report them.
cannot_establish: That gabapentinoids rarely cause dependence or do not contribute to deaths (no data on people taking gabapentinoids are presented: the 0.5% and 0.25% are of all patients in a hospital sample of older people); that they protect people who use opioids by replacing riskier drugs (the authors say this has not been investigated); or how safe they are compared with other drugs (expert opinion).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). Data cited from the authors' own work: 400 patients from the elderly population of a German metropolitan general hospital, interviewed face to face with the DSM-IV-based SKID-I (Bonnet, Strasser and Scherbaum, 2019, Addictive Behaviors 90:265–271, as summarized); ratings of harms and benefits by 101 German physicians specialized in addiction medicine (Bonnet et al., 2020 and 2021, as summarized) (pp. 611–612).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selected by the authors; all new data offered come from their own group (refs 7–10), and their two earlier reviews are cited for central points (refs 11, 22). The hospital sample is of older inpatients in one German metropolitan area; the experts are German addiction physicians, whose view the authors say may not apply to countries with an opioid epidemic (p. 612, 2nd paragraph and Fig. 1 legend).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at letter level. In the cited hospital study, dependence on gabapentinoids and on other non-opioid analgesics was assessed face to face with the SKID-I (DSM-IV) (pp. 611–612); how many of the 400 patients took gabapentinoids is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the argument: the letter says the evidence of harm comes from people dependent on opioids and other substances (p. 611), and proposes, without data, that gabapentinoids might protect such people by replacing riskier co-used drugs (p. 612).

outcomes.instruments: SKID-I (German version of the SCID-I) for DSM-IV dependence in the cited hospital study; experts' ratings of total harm and of benefit (Fig. 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Dependence by DSM-IV criteria, graded mild to moderate; harm as an expert-rated total-harm score; benefit as the share of ratings 'no or little benefit'.

analysis.effect_sizes: As reported for the authors' own studies: among 400 elderly hospital patients, 28 (7%) were dependent on other non-opioid analgesics (mainly NSAIDs and metamizole), 2 (0.5%) reported newly developed gabapentinoid dependence (mild to moderate) together with such analgesic dependence, and 1 (0.25%) had isolated gabapentinoid dependence, rated mild, in a man previously dependent on opioids (pp. 611–612). Expert ratings, read approximately from Fig. 1 (p. 612): gabapentinoids at a total-harm score of about 1.1 with about 7% of ratings 'no or little benefit', against benzodiazepines about 1.9 and 9%, alcohol about 2.7 and 45%, heroin about 3.1 and 60%.
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter does not engage with the specific associations the review reports (for example, overdose death in opioid maintenance), and presents its own favourable data without their limits (for example, how many of the 400 patients took gabapentinoids).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The letter adds no new systematic data. Its one set of patient figures comes from a hospital sample of older people in which the number taking gabapentinoids is not given, so 0.5% and 0.25% are proportions of all patients, not risks among people taking gabapentinoids; the harm-benefit plot is the opinion of addiction physicians in one country.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Its criticism of the review is mainly methodological and reasonable: observational data cannot establish causation, the samples are mostly opioid-dependent, outcomes are often surrogate, and no study accounted for confounders well enough to support a causal link (p. 611); the review's own Limitations concede most of this. Its own conclusions go further than its evidence: gabapentinoids are called highly useful and rather safe, and considerably safer among people with other addictions because of a wide therapeutic window (pp. 612–613), and further concern is called "unfounded castigation" (p. 613), although the letter concedes that a combined respiratory-depressant effect has been neither proven nor excluded and that the substitution hypothesis has not been investigated (pp. 612–613), and it does not address the opioid-overdose associations the review reports. It also describes its own cross-sectional screening study as a cross-over study of randomized patients (reporting issue).

timeline.event: Cossmann, Scherbaum and Bonnet, GeroPsych 29(1):17–27: cross-sectional study of 400 inpatients aged 65 or more in a German general hospital, cited in the 2017 review with one lifetime case of gabapentin dependence (no project record).
The letter authors' own systematic review of how addictive gabapentinoids are (ref 11)

Bonnet, Strasser and Scherbaum, Addictive Behaviors 90:265–271: screening for dependence on non-opioid analgesics in a German elderly hospital population, the source of the letter's 400-patient figures (ref 7; not among the files read; no project record).
The systematic review update the letter comments on
The review authors' reply to the letter (Drugs; DOI 10.1007/s40265-021-01495-0), not among the files read.

replication.where_it_stands: A published critique, by authors of an earlier review on the same question, of the causal and generalizing language in Evoy et al. (2021). It identifies no factual or numerical error in the review's tables; its strongest points (no causal analysis, opioid-dependent samples, surrogate outcomes) are conceded in the review's own Limitations. The authors' reply has not been read.

funding.funder: Open Access funding enabled and organized by Projekt DEAL (Declarations, p. 613).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest related to this letter, except that they had carried out two reviews about the harms and addiction of pregabalin and gabapentin (refs 11, 22). Norbert Scherbaum received honoraria for advisory boards, lectures and manuscripts from AbbVie, Camurus, Hexal, Janssen-Cilag, MSD, Medice, Mundipharma, Reckitt-Benckiser/Indivior and Sanofi-Aventis, and during the last 3 years participated in clinical trials financed by the pharmaceutical industry (p. 613).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Evangelisches Krankenhaus Castrop-Rauxel (teaching hospital of the University of Duisburg-Essen) and LVR-Hospital Essen (University of Duisburg-Essen), Germany; Northern Anesthesia and Pain Medicine LLC (Eagle River, Alaska) and the Department of Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine, University of Washington (p. 611). The authors are clinicians who use gabapentinoids in addiction and pain medicine, and the letter argues against restricting supply. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the letter.

what_would_settle_it: Well-powered prospective cohorts, with confounders measured, comparing psychological dependence and deaths in people taking gabapentinoids with and without opioid dependence (the letter's own proposal, p. 611), or randomized studies where feasible; and a study of whether gabapentinoids replace or add to riskier drugs among people who use opioids.

domains.note: No search beyond one PubMed query for mediation analyses (p. 611); sources chosen by the authors.

Criticizes the review's evidence base in general terms (designs, samples, surrogate outcomes) but appraises no individual study, and does not appraise its own studies (for example, the number of the 400 patients taking gabapentinoids).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: All new data offered are the authors' own (refs 7–10), and their earlier reviews are cited for central points (refs 11, 22).

The substitution hypothesis is labelled as not investigated and the respiratory interaction as unproven (pp. 612–613), but considerable safety among people with other addictions and overall safety are stated as findings without data in the letter.

domains.domain: Balance of harms against benefits of gabapentinoids
domains.note: Benefits in withdrawal treatment and the authors' favourable expert ratings are presented in detail; the specific mortality and hospital associations reported in the review are not discussed, so the evidence of harm is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS 5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domains (search and reliance on the authors' own studies). The letter is useful for the methodological objections to the review, which are reasonable and largely conceded in the review's own Limitations, and as a pointer to the authors' hospital study. It is not a source for how safe gabapentinoids are: its safety statements rest on expert opinion and on the authors' own unappraised data. Cite it for what the critics argue, not for figures on dependence, which should come from the primary study.

key_findings.finding: The letter accepts the limits the review itself states: small samples, mostly retrospective designs, and homogeneous cohorts of people dependent on opioids and other substances; clinical studies of people without past or present substance use disorders are lacking.

The authors argue that the reported outcomes are relatively rare and often surrogate, and that they know of only a minuscule number of people worldwide seeking treatment for gabapentinoid misuse or addiction; a widely used, strongly addictive drug would, they argue, have produced a substantial group seeking detoxification, which has not been seen.

Causation: the authors know of no study that accounted for predictors and confounders well enough to support a causal link between gabapentinoid use or misuse and harms including psychological dependence and death; a PubMed search combining mediation analysis with gabapentin or pregabalin and harm terms found no human studies; among the review's 46 new observational studies only very few prospective investigations addressed gabapentinoid addiction and deaths, and those were small, less specific or limited to people using opioids; they call for well-powered controlled prospective studies comparing dependence and deaths in opioid-dependent and general-population samples. [The letter does not say that very few of the 46 were prospective overall.]

From the authors' own study of 400 patients in the elderly population of a German metropolitan general hospital, assessed with the DSM-IV-based SKID-I: 28 (7%) were dependent on other non-opioid analgesics (mainly NSAIDs and metamizole); 2 (0.5%) reported newly developed gabapentinoid dependence (mild to moderate) together with such analgesic dependence; 1 (0.25%) had isolated gabapentinoid dependence, a man previously dependent on opioids whose current gabapentin dependence was rated mild.
key_findings.note: The denominator is all 400 patients, not those taking gabapentinoids, and the design words used for this study are inaccurate (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In an expert ranking by German addiction physicians, gabapentinoids ranked at the low end of physical, psychological and social harm to the people who use them and to others; Fig. 1 (101 physicians specialized in addiction medicine, median 15 years in tertiary care) plots harm against benefit, and the authors say this view may not generalize to countries with an opioid epidemic. On the editors' reading of Fig. 1, gabapentinoids sit at a total-harm score of about 1.1 with about 7% of ratings 'no or little benefit', near buprenorphine and NSAIDs and below benzodiazepines (about 1.9) and alcohol (about 2.7).
key_findings.note: Values read from Fig. 1 on a 300-dpi rendering (approximate); this is expert opinion, not measured harm.

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that a good portion of the patients admitted to their own detoxification units from illicit drugs, mostly opioids, also use gabapentinoids.

Gabapentinoids may give euphoria and relaxation, especially at doses above the therapeutic range; the authors assert a wide therapeutic window and propose that they might protect people who misuse opioids by replacing higher-risk co-used drugs (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, promethazine, NSAIDs, paracetamol, alcohol), adding that this has not been investigated.

Benefits cited: easing withdrawal from alcohol (evidence levels II–Ia) and opioids (II–Ib) and, in one randomized trial, cannabis (Ib); the authors also note that relief of withdrawal can itself be rewarding and lead to psychological dependence.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph of p. 612 (right column, continues on p. 613)

key_findings.finding: Harms acknowledged: gabapentinoids may raise the risk of adverse outcomes in people who use other substances through synergistic depression of the central nervous system and perhaps of breathing; the letter says 'the latter' has been proven neither mechanistically nor clinically; reversal of tolerance to the sedative and breathing-depressant effects of the abused drug is called a substantial concern. ['The latter' most naturally means the respiratory part. The card's own interpretation-gap text reads it that way, but this finding applied it to the whole combined effect.]

Conclusion: prescribing needs careful individual benefit-risk assessment, monitoring and tapering when risks begin to outweigh benefits; from the authors' clinical view gabapentinoids are highly useful and rather safe, including in addiction medicine; controlled prospective observational or randomized studies are needed before "further unfounded castigation".

The letter points to no specific numerical or factual error in the review; its objections concern study design, causal inference, generalization from opioid-dependent samples and the balance of harms against benefits.
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the full letter. Errors in the review's text found on reading it (for example the mislabelled hazard ratios and the country of one cohort) are recorded on sc_evoy_2021.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter calls its own study "a clinical cross-over study" of 400 randomized patients (pp. 611–612), but its reference 7 is titled as screening for dependence in a hospital population, and the same authors' 2017 review cites what appears to be the same sample (400 inpatients aged 65 or more in a German general hospital) as a cross-sectional study (Cossmann et al., 2016, titled as a cross-sectional study in a German hospital; Bonnet and Scherbaum, 2017, Table 1 and references, PDF pp. 5, 27).
reporting_issues.consequence: The design words suggest an experiment; the study appears to be a cross-sectional screening survey in which randomized probably means randomly selected. A claim must not call it a trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The counts differ from the authors' 2017 account of what appears to be the same sample: the 2017 review reports one person with transient gabapentin dependence (lifetime prevalence 0.25%, 12-month prevalence 0%) and no case with pregabalin (Bonnet and Scherbaum, 2017, Table 1, PDF p. 5), while the letter reports three people with gabapentinoid dependence (two alongside dependence on other non-opioid analgesics, one isolated) and calls the isolated case's dependence current.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unless the 2019 paper re-analysed the sample or used a different one, the two accounts cannot both be right; the primary paper (Bonnet, Strasser and Scherbaum, 2019) is needed before either figure is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportions 0.5% and 0.25% are of all 400 patients; the letter does not say how many were taking or had taken gabapentinoids.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are not risks of dependence among people taking gabapentinoids and cannot be set against the review's rates in opioid-treatment samples.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter summarizes the review's conclusion as gabapentinoid misuse growing and comprising a significant individual and public health threat (p. 611); the review's abstract says misuse is a growing trend causing significant patient harm (Evoy et al., 2021, PDF p. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor paraphrase; the review's claim is about harm to patients, not a public-health threat.
